REASONS FOR DECISION 14.
In the present case, prosecution has examined 7 witnesses in total to prove its case against the accused Gajender Singh.

Before appreciating the evidence on record, it is important to examine the necessary ingredients for offence under Section 279/304-A IPC which are as follows:-
(1) That the accident actually took place.
(2) That the accident took place due to rash and negligent driving.
(3) That the accused was the person who was driving the vehicle at the relevant time.

sentences.text: That words i.e. "rash" and "negligent", have not been defined in the Indian Penal Code.

However,
as per Blacks Law Dictionary, Eighth Edition the work 'Negligent' is characterized by a person's failure to exercise the degree of care that someone of ordinary prudence would have exercised in the same circumstance.

State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
4

Quoting from the article "Negligence, Mens Rea and Criminal Responsibility" by H.L.A. Hart in Punishment and Responsibility the dictionary further goes on to explain the difference between an act done inadvertently and an act done negligently.

"[A] careful consideration is needed of the difference between the meeting of the expression like 'inadvertently' and 'while his mind was a blank' on the one hand, and 'negligently' on the other hand.

In ordinary English, and also in Lawyer's English,
when harm has resulted from someone's negligence, if we say of that person that he has acted negligently we are not thereby merely describing the frame of mind in which he acted.
'He negligently broke a saucer' is not the same kind of expression as 'he inadvertently broke a saucer'.

The point of adverb 'inadvertently' is merely to inform us of the agent's psychological state, whereas if we say 'He broke it negligently' we are not merely adding to this an element of blame or reproach, but something quite specific, viz.

We are referring to the fact that the agent failed to comply CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 8 of 17 with a standard man could and would have complied:
a standard requiring him to take precautions against harm.

entities.text: CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 8 of 17
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The work 'negligently',
both in legal and non lelgal contexts, makes an essential reference to an omission to do what is thus required: it is not a flatly descriptive psychological expression like 'his mind was a blank'."
16.
The Oxford Advances Learner's Dictionary, Sixth Edition defines 'Rash' as doing something that may not be sensible without first thinking about the possible results.

Elaborating further, in State of H.P. V. Piar Chand, Cr. Appeal No. 109 of 2003, decided on 02.06.2003, Himachal Pradesh High Court, while dealing with the meaning of the expression "rashness" and "negligence" held as follows:
"18. Criminal rashness is doing a dangerous or wanton act with the knowledge that it is so and may cause injury but without intention to cause injury and without knowledge that injury would probably be caused.

entities.text: State of H.P. V. Piar Chand
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Therefore, to incur criminal liability, the act must be done with rashness or indifference as to the consequence.

Criminal negligence is the gross and culpable neglect or failure to exercise reasonable care and proper precaution imperative to be adopted by a person to avoid causing of injury to the public or a person or an individual."
CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 9 of 17 17.

entities.text: CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The distinction has been very aptly pointed out by Holloway, J. in these words:
"Culpable rashness is acting with the consciousness that the mischievous and illegal consequences may follow, but with the hope that they will not, and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.

The State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
5
imputability arises from acting despite the consciousness.

Culpable negligence is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow,
but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon his and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the negligence of the civic duty of circumspection."
(see in Re: Nidamorti Nagabhushanam 7 Mad. HCR 119)".
18. The prosecution in the present case was required to show enough evidence on record to establish that the conduct of the accused was either rash or negligent under the given fact situation.

It is the case of the prosecution that accused Gajender Singh while driving Bus bearing No. DL-1PA-6932 (hereinafter referred to as offending vehicle) in a rash and negligent manner hit against an aged pedestrian namely Hari and caused his death and thus he committed offences punishable under Section 279/304A IPC.
CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 10 of 17 19.

sentences.text: In his statement u/s 313 Cr.PC, the accused had admitted that he was driving the offending vehicle on the date of incident, however, he had taken the plea that he had not caused the accident.
In such circumstances, the fact that the offending vehicle was being driven by the accused is not required to be proved by the prosecution.
20. The accused vide his statement u/s 294 Cr.PC admitted postmortem report of the deceased Hari Ram.
Thus, it stands established that the deceased Hari Ram succumbed to the injuries caused by the accident.
Hence, what remains to be established is whether the accident was caused by the rash or negligent act of the accused on the said date, time and place.
21. The role of a witness is paramount in the criminal justice delivery system.
A witness has relevant information about a crime and important constituent of the administration of justice.
A witness by giving evidence relating to the commission of an offence performs a sacred duty of assisting the court to discover the truth.
The prosecution does not require number of eye witnesses to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.

Even if there is one eye witness and his testimony is upto the mark,
the conviction can be based upon the same.

22. The fact which is required to be proved beyond any reasonable doubt in a case u/s 304A IPC is the fact of rash and negligent driving by the accused persons and proving this fact is germane to the CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 11 of 17 conviction of a person u/s 304A.

entities.text: CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 11 of 17
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 23. As per the case of the prosecution, Ct. Vinod Kumar (PW2) was the eye witness of the incident as he was at the beat duty and had witnessed the accident.
24. At the outset, it has to be noted that the presence of the witness at the spot has been disputed by the Ld. Counsel for accused.

It is pertinent to mention that the prosecution had relied upon the fact that PW2 Ct. Vinod Kumar was present at Bhajanpura in Bhajanpura Beat and he had witnessed the State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
6 incident at about 10:00 AM.
However, Roznamcha register has not been brought on record to show that the said witness had left the PS for performing beat duty.
This fact raises the doubt regarding the presence of the witness at the spot.
24.1 It is also pertinent to refer to the testimony of this very important witness.
PW2 Ct. Vinod Kumar had stated in his examination in chief that the site plan was prepared at his instance.
However, in his cross-examination, the witness stated that the site plan was not prepared at his instance.
It is also noteworthy that the witness stated that IO had himself prepared the site plan and that his position is not shown in the site plan.

Further, the witness stated that the IO had not enquired from any public person in his presence and then again he stated that IO had enquired from the passengers of the bus regarding the manner of accident.
Thus, the said witness had not remained consistent regarding the material particulars of the case.
The site plan Ex.PW2/B has been casually prepared by the IO wherein the position of the eye witness has CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS:
Khajuri Khas Page no. 12 of 17 not been shown which also indicates towards the absence of this witness at the spot.

In such cases of road accidents, the site plan is required to be prepared very carefully by properly mentioning as to where the victim was standing and from where the accused was coming and the same must also mention the spot of presence of eye witness, if any.
It is further to be seen that the witness PW2 stated that the vehicle was being driven in a very fast speed and in a rash and negligent manner.

25. The Supreme Court in State of Karnataka V Satish, 1998 SCC (Crl) 1508 observed as under:-
"Both the trial court and the appellate court held the respon- dent guilty for offences under Section 337, 338 and 304A IPC after recording a finding that the respondent was driving the truck at a "high speed".

entities.text: State of Karnataka V Satish, 1998 SCC (Crl) 1508
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: No specific finding has been recorded either by the trial court or by the first appellate court to the effect that the respondent was driving the truck either negligently or rashly.
After holding that the respon- dent was driving the truck at a "high speed", both the courts pressed into aid the doctrine of res ipsa loquitor to hold the respondent guilty.
Merely because the truck was being driven at a "high speed" does not bespeak of either "negligence" or "rashness" by itself.

None of the witnesses examined by the prosecution could give any indication,
even approximately, as to what they meant by "high speed".
"High speed" is a relative term.
It was for the prosecution to bring on record material to establish as to what is meant by "high speed" in the facts and circumstances of the case.

In a criminal trial,
the burden of proving everything essential to the establishment of the charge against an CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 13 of 17 accused always rests on the prosecution and there is a presumption of innocence in favor of the accused until the contrary is proved.

entities.text: CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 13 of 17
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Criminality is not to be presumed,
subject of course to some statutory exceptions.
There is no such statutory exception pleaded in the present case.

In the absence of any material on the record, no presumption of "rashness" or "negligence" could be drawn by invoking the maxim "res ipsa loquitor"".
State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
7 26.

At this stage, it is pertinent to mention that in the case titled "Abdul Subhan vs State (NCT of Delhi)" 2006 (4) LRC 472 (Del)", it was held by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi as below:-
"High speed by itself may not in each case be sufficient to hold that the driver is rash and negligent.

entities.text: Abdul Subhan vs State (NCT of Delhi)" 2006 (4) LRC 472 (Del)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Speed alone is not a criteria for deciding the rashness or negligence on the part of the driver".
27. Apart from stating that the accused was driving the vehicle in a high speed, PW2 did not state anything as to how the accused was rash or negligent.
PW2 has also not stated anything regarding the manner in which the vehicle was being driven.

28. Further, it is noted that the investigation officer i.e. PW6 had not recorded statement of any public witness, though it is stated by PW2 CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 14 of 17 Ct. Vinod Kumar that passengers of the bus were enquired by the IO regarding the manner of accident.

entities.text: CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 14 of 17
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There are no photographs of the spot on record and the photographs of the offending vehicle and the mechanical inspection report do not offer any assistance in arriving to the conclusion that the accused was rash or negligent while driving the said vehicle.
29.1 The act of rashness or negligence has remained unproved on record which is the primary requirement for recording conviction in such cases.
There is no explanation on record as to why Roznamcha register /relevant entries were not produced on record to substantiate the factum of presence of PW2 at the spot.
The contradictions in the testimony of PW2 regarding preparation of site plan also creates a dent in the story of the prosecution.

As per the reply to this notice u/s 133 MV Act, the accused was produced by PW Rajender Singh in the PS on 12.03.2009 itself whereas the arrest memo of the accused mentions the date of arrest as 14.03.2009.
29.2

Reading the testimonies of the witnesses as a whole and considering the evidence led by the prosecution, there is a reasonable doubt regarding the culpability of the accused and the alleged rashness or negligence on his part as opposed to the allegations levelled against him.
30. It has been held in case of Sadhu Singh V/s State of Punjab 1997(3) Crime 55 the Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court :-

entities.text: Sadhu Singh V/s State of Punjab 1997(3) Crime 55
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
"In a criminal trial, it is for the prosecution to CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs.
Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 15 of 17 establish its case beyond all reasonable doubts.

entities.text:
CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs.
Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 15 of 17
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is for the prosecution to travel the entire distance from may have to must have.

If the prosecution appears to be improbable or lacks credibility the benefit of doubt necessarily has to go to the accused."
31.

In the considered opinion of this court, it shall not be safe to convict the accused in the present case and accordingly benefit of doubt shall be afforded to him as presence of the only eye witness i.e.
PW2 has not been established conclusively by the prosecution at the spot and the site plan prepared by the IO appears to have been prepared casually.

Even the eye witness in his cross-examination State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
8 stated that the site plan had not prepared at his instance.
32. Thus considering the above mentioned reasons, the court has come to the conclusion that prosecution has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Thus, as prosecution failed to prove that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent act of accused Gajender Singh, he deserves to be acquitted.

Hence, accused Gajender Singh is acquitted for the offences punishable u/s 279/304A IPC.
33.
In view of the acquittal of the accused, it is deemed fit to direct for consideration of appropriate compensation of the victim /LRs of deceased in terms of Section 357A(3) Cr.PC.

For the said purpose, this CS No. 462910/2015 State Vs. Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 16 of 17 court recommends that the victim be given compensation as per the various scheme pertaining to compensation of the Government.

Gajender Singh PS: Khajuri Khas Page no. 13 of 17 accused always rests on the prosecution and there is a presumption of innocence in favor of the accused until the contrary is proved.
Criminality is not to be presumed,
subject of course to some statutory exceptions.
In the absence of any material on the record, no presumption of "rashness" or "negligence" could be drawn by invoking the maxim "res ipsa loquitor"".
State vs . Gajender Singh on 19 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69421869/
7 26.
The contradictions in the testimony of PW2 regarding preparation of site plan also creates a dent in the story of the prosecution.
Reading the testimonies of the witnesses as a whole and considering the evidence led by the prosecution, there is a reasonable doubt regarding the culpability of the accused and the alleged rashness or negligence on his part as opposed to the allegations levelled against him.
30. It has been held in case of Sadhu Singh V/s State of Punjab 1997(3) Crime 55 the Hon'ble Punjab & Haryana High Court :-
In the considered opinion of this court, it shall not be safe to convict the accused in the present case and accordingly benefit of doubt shall be afforded to him as presence of the only eye witness i.e.
PW2 has not been established conclusively by the prosecution at the spot and the site plan prepared by the IO appears to have been prepared casually.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Hence, accused Gajender Singh is acquitted for the offences punishable u/s 279/304A IPC.
33.
In view of the acquittal of the accused, it is deemed fit to direct for consideration of appropriate compensation of the victim /LRs of deceased in terms of Section 357A(3) Cr.PC.
Let copy of this judgment be also sent to Ld. Secretary, DLSA for information and for providing the compensation to the injured/victim.
34. Copy of this judgment be given free of cost to accused against receiving.
Let copy of this judgment be also sent to the victim/LRs of the deceased through the concerned SHO.
